verdicts.claim: The public hooks exist with no edits needed: FrontRooms3DGame.MapRunStarted(FrontRoomsMapWorld, FrontRoomsMapHunter), MapRunEnded and PlayerClimbed; the map events DoorMoved, GlassBroken, DoorBroken, KeyTaken, GlassHold, GlassHoldReleased and DoorLocked; the queries PassageBetween, DoorBetween, CellOf, CellCenter, ZoneOf, IsBuilt, InStartArea, SightDistance and Cache; on the Relay, Position, State, SeesPlayer and the StateChanged, DoorBlow and Caught events.
verdicts.evidence: FrontRooms3DGame.cs:39-43 declares the three static events, and MapRunStarted is invoked at :601. FrontRoomsMapWorld.cs:59-71 declares the events, :74 has enum Passage {Open, Wall, ClosedDoor, Glass}, :94-104 has public sealed class Door with public open/broken/progress, :41 has public Cache, and :510-522 and :978/:1001 hold the queries. FrontRoomsMapHunter.cs:107-128 has the public State/Position/Heading/Moving/SeesPlayer and the StateChanged/DoorBlow/Caught events.

verdicts.claim: buildRadius is 2 (5x5 chunks, 120 m). The 3x3 ring is only ReadyAround(1). Camera far plane = SightDistance = buildRadius*24-2 = 46 m. 1 lamp in 3 casts shadows; lightRadius 16, shadowRadius 9.
verdicts.evidence: FrontRoomsLevel0.asset:44,48,49 has buildRadius 2, lightRadius 16, shadowRadius 9. FrontRoomsMapWorld.cs:56 has SightDistance => BuildRadius*ChunkSize-2. The 0.34 shadow chance is at :1069. However, FrontRooms3DGame.cs:225 sets farClipPlane = 80 at creation, and :720-722 only clamps it to SightDistance outside the start rooms. Inside the stream rooms it can be larger: Clamp(..., SightDistance, SightDistance + distance to door).
verdicts.correction: The far plane is 46 m only during map play outside the stream rooms. In the start rooms it is at least 46 m and can be longer, so the far plane alone cannot be the 'unseen' bound there.

verdicts.claim: PlanarFrame sets t = normalize(cross(up,n)) and u = dot(positionWS,t), so u = -z on +X faces, +z on -X, +x on +Z and -x on -Z. Strip seams fall on world multiples of 0.75 m on both faces, and the wallpaper tile is 0.75 x 1.125 m.
verdicts.evidence: FrontRoomsSurface.shader:157-162 matches. Working it out: cross((0,1,0),(1,0,0)) = (0,0,-1), so u = -z on +X faces. The tile is set by RenderSetup:272-278, tile = (Roll, Roll*1.5) for L0_Wallpaper, L0_Wallpaper_Shift and Exit_Wallpaper. Caveat: the shader also multiplies by _BaseMap_ST (:183), so strip math must use metres, not the final uv. Materials with the _FR_MESH_UV keyword bypass PlanarFrame entirely.

verdicts.claim: gen_surfaces.wallpaper() bakes ink into height (0.9*blur(ink)), smoothness (+0.07*ink) and cavity (-0.10*ink), and the roll-seam shadow sits at the texture x=0/W edges. MaskMap A is unused.
verdicts.evidence: gen_surfaces.py wallpaper(): seam_shadow is computed from dd = min(x, W-x). Height includes .9*blur(ink,1.2), smooth includes .07*blur(ink,1.0), and cav includes -.10*ink. mask() (gen_surfaces.py:17-19) writes A = ones, and gen_common.py:9 documents A as unused. The A channel exists (RGBA PNG) but currently holds a constant 1, so any fibre threshold field would have to be generated. Texture import: Default platform maxTextureSize 4096, other platforms not overridden, so 2048x3072 survives and the 0.37 mm texel figure holds.

verdicts.claim: The DepthNormals pass uses URP's generic DepthNormalsPass.hlsl and writes the interpolated geometric normal (no normal map), so SSAO ignores both the paper normal and the print. ShadowCaster is depth-only.
verdicts.evidence: FrontRoomsSurface.shader:302-316 includes Packages/.../Shaders/DepthNormalsPass.hlsl with no _NORMALMAP define. The local URP 17.3.0 DepthNormalsPass.hlsl fragment writes NormalizeNormalPerPixel(input.normalWS) and has no NORMALMAP branch at all. ShadowCaster includes ShadowCasterPass.hlsl (:266-281).

verdicts.claim: In URP, _Time = (t/20, t, 2t, 3t) and matches Time.time, the time since application start. Only Built-In uses timeSinceLevelLoad. So _Time does not reset on scene reload.
verdicts.evidence: The Unity 6000.3 manual says: 'Time matches Time.time, which is the time since the application started. If you use the Built-In Render Pipeline, time matches Time.timeSinceLevelLoad instead.' The precision arithmetic is also right: float ulp at 3600 s is 2^-12 = 0.24 ms, and at 86400 s it is 2^-7 = 7.8 ms.

verdicts.claim: Fog is ExponentialSquared at density 0.014 and URP computes factor = exp(-(density*z)^2), so walls at 20 m are about 93% unfogged and walls at 46 m about 66%.
verdicts.evidence: FrontRoomsLook.cs:19 and :32-34 set FogMode.ExponentialSquared with FogDensity .014. URP ShaderVariablesFunctions.hlsl implements exp2(-fogFactor^2) with the comment 'factor = exp(-(density*z)^2)'. One nuance: z is clip/view depth, not radial distance, so fog at screen edges (108° horizontal FOV) is even weaker than these figures. The conclusion that fog cannot hide changes holds.

verdicts.claim: Decision-2 shifted chunks are rebuilt at least 24 m away and, in practice, past the 46 m far plane, because they rebuild as they re-enter ring 2.
verdicts.evidence: FrontRoomsMapWorld.cs Stream(): Cache.Shift(coord) runs inside the build loop when Time.time - droppedAt >= shiftAfterSeconds, and the comment says 'always at least one chunk (24 m) away'. Re-entry happens when the player crosses into a new centre chunk, which puts the new ring-2 chunk 48 m or more away along the axis. But builds are budgeted (chunksPerFrame = 1), so a ring-2 chunk can be built several frames after the crossing, when the player is closer than 48 m. A ring-1 chunk that was dropped can also shift if the player was away long enough.
verdicts.correction: The guaranteed bound is 24 m or more (one chunk), which is inside the 46 m far plane. Being 'past the far plane' is typical but not guaranteed, so the print should not rely on it being unseen without the visibility test.

verdicts.claim: Renderer.isVisible counts as visible when rendered only for shadows and when Scene view cameras see it. CullingGroup uses frustum plus static occlusion only and cannot re-query immediately after scene changes. TestPlanesAABB is conservative, with false positives.
verdicts.evidence: Renderer.isVisible page: 'might not actually be visible by any camera but still need to be rendered for shadows... Scene view cameras will also cause this value to be true.' CullingGroup page: 'frustum culling and static occlusion culling only', and it 'does not give you the ability to make changes to your scene and then immediately request the new visibility state'. TestPlanesAABB page: 'The test is conservative and can give false positive results.'

verdicts.claim: Target 3.5 = OpenGL ES 3.0 with integers. Random write from pixel shaders (SetRandomWriteTarget) needs target 4.5. The existing shader is target 3.5.
verdicts.evidence: SL-Pragma-target: 3.5 'Equivalent to OpenGL ES 3.0', and 4.5 adds 'compute randomwrite msaatex'. The SetRandomWriteTarget page targets 'Shader Model 4.5 level pixel shaders'. FrontRoomsSurface.shader has #pragma target 3.5 in all passes (:88, :276, :294, :310). The integer ops (&, uint hashes) in the sketch are allowed at 3.5.

verdicts.claim: A global is used only when the material does not define the property, so _FR_* must stay out of Properties and UnityPerMaterial. SetGlobalVectorArray fixes the array length on first set.
verdicts.evidence: The 6000.3 SetGlobalVectorArray page confirms 'Global properties are used if a shader needs them but the material does not have them defined.' It says nothing about the array length being fixed on first use, and the report already flags that as unconfirmed. (Older Unity docs for MaterialPropertyBlock/Shader arrays state the size cannot change after first set, but that was not checked against 6000.3 here.)
verdicts.correction: Treat the fixed-length behaviour as unverified for 6000.3. Always sending the full 8 is still the safe practice.

verdicts.claim: MaterialPropertyBlocks make a renderer SRP-Batcher-incompatible, and the map already sets _CeilingHeight per shell renderer via an MPB.
verdicts.evidence: The SRP Batcher materials page says: 'The GameObject mustn't use MaterialPropertyBlocks.' FrontRoomsMapWorld.cs around :745-770 creates new MaterialPropertyBlock() with CeilingHeightId and calls r.SetPropertyBlock(props).

verdicts.claim: Lamp temperaments are 62% steady, 20% stutter, 10% failing, 5% dead-with-blinks, 3% dim. Relay noise radii are sprint 26 m, door 14 m, glass 40 m. Strontium aluminate dates from 1993 (Nemoto) and is about 10x brighter and longer than Cu:ZnS.
verdicts.evidence: FrontRoomsMapWorld.cs: fixture.mode = roll < .62 ? 0 : < .82 ? 1 : < .92 ? 2 : < .97 ? 3 : 4. FrontRoomsHunter.cs:29-30 has sprintNoiseRadius 26 and doorNoiseRadius 14. FrontRooms3DGame.cs:148 has GlassNoiseRadius = 40. Wikipedia: developed in 1993 by Aoki at Nemoto, patent filed 1994, 'approximately 10 times greater than zinc sulfide'.

verdicts.claim: Minor code citations: Time.timeScale is set to 1 at FrontRooms3DGame.cs:295, and the game calls relay.Noise for sprint directly at :854.
verdicts.evidence: Actual lines: Time.timeScale = 1f is at :294, and the sprint call `if (sprinting) relay?.Noise(playerRoot.position, hunterTuning.sprintNoiseRadius)` is at :858. Door noise is at :781 and glass at :788.
verdicts.correction: The lines are off by 1-4. The substance is correct: no sprint-noise event exists, and the game calls relay.Noise directly.

verdicts.claim: The map root always sits on a multiple of 192 m. The game's root is near the origin (hundreds of metres), so precision does not matter there.
verdicts.evidence: MapRootFor (FrontRooms3DGame.cs:607-630) searches roots a*192, b*192 for rings up to 24, so the root is always on a 192 m multiple. LEVEL_MODULE_SPEC §5 says 'The game's map root is at the origin', but the code can pick a root up to 24*192 = 4608 m away when nearer roots fail its door test.
verdicts.correction: The root is usually near the origin, but the search allows up to about 4.6 km, the same float band as the 4992 m test root. Treat the precision note as relevant to real play, not just to captures.

gaps: The visibility pass fails in the start/stream rooms. PassageBetween returns Wall whenever either cell is InStartArea, and IsBuilt is false for start cells. A camera in the stream room standing at the open stream door therefore marks no map cell visible, yet it can see into the maze (the far plane there can exceed 46 m). The report does gate the stream rooms to subliminal-only, but the C# sketch does not enforce it. The BFS needs a seed: the start-door cell plus the frustum-tested cells beyond it.

Toroidal aliasing outside map cells: the stream rooms physically occupy start-area cells and are world geometry, not map cells. Their wallpaper will read texels (cell & 63) that alias live map cells 64 cells away. Saying 'leave them neutral' does not happen on its own; the shader needs a material keyword or a mask so stream-room and office walls skip the lookup.

Cache.IsBuilt(chunk) means 'present in the generation cache', not 'built in the scene'. Cache.Get on an uncached chunk generates it (a side effect), and ZoneOf and Edge queries also fill the cache. Change detection should use map.IsBuilt and the drop/build transitions, not Cache.IsBuilt.

Shifted chunks are guaranteed only to be 24 m or more away (one chunk), not beyond the far plane. chunksPerFrame budgeting can delay builds, so the claim that decision-2 rebuilds are a 'free, guaranteed-unseen moment' needs the same frustum/BFS check.

The probe (positionWS + n*0.5) assumes axis-aligned wall faces on 3 m lines. Furniture, door leaves, window frames or reveals sharing the wallpaper material, and any _FR_MESH_UV mesh, are not checked. With _FR_MESH_UV the strip index from PlanarFrame u does not exist.

Uploading State/Field textures (SetPixelData + Apply) and setting globals inside beginCameraRendering was not verified against URP 17 ordering. Depth/shadow passes for that camera are recorded after the callback, so this is probably fine, but it is unverified. Multiple cameras (UI, capture tools) would each trigger the callback; the report filters to Camera.main only.

The BFS ignores sight lines through Tall (5.4 m) halls over lower walls, and ignores whether windows/glass in walls of different heights are see-through. It also treats closed doors as opaque even though door leaves might have glass panes. None of this was checked in the module spec.

No cited Unity source confirms that RenderPipelineManager.beginCameraRendering runs after the camera transform is final for the frame (the mouse look applied in Update/LateUpdate). This is needed for the 'snap before first visible frame' guarantee. It is likely true but was not checked.
The SetGlobalVectorArray fixed-length behaviour and 'URP does not render camera-relative' are stated without a Unity 6 source.
The report's precision note assumes the root is near the origin, but MapRootFor can place it up to about 4.6 km away, so float quantisation of motion-layer UVs is a real-play concern.

report.summary: I verified 30+ precedents with working URLs across film, literature, games, real-world materials and 1990-era technology. The main result is that the user's "sandwich" (a changing graphic under a static material skin that alone carries lighting and reflections) has direct physical precedents. These are E Ink film (E Ink Prism 2015, BMW iX Flow 2022), lenticular prints, Philips/Kvadrat Luminous Textile (2011), Meystyle LED wallpaper (2004/2007) and thermochromic wallpapers (Shi Yuan, by 2008; Sibren Drenthen 2019). Pablo Valbuena's Augmented Sculpture (2007) states the two-layer idea almost word for word: a physical layer plus a projected layer that controls transformation. The narrative precedent is Gilman's "The Yellow Wallpaper" (1892). Its wallpaper is literally two layers: a front pattern, and a sub-pattern in a different shade that shows "only in certain lights" and moves by moonlight while staying still by day. Kane Parsons' own Backrooms series links to it: episode 13 is titled with the story's ISBN, and episode 24 shows "stretched wallpaper". The best trigger precedent is Disneyland's Haunted Mansion (1969), where portraits flicker into macabre versions when lightning flashes. That maps directly onto FrontRooms' independently flickering troffers. Games add more trigger types: change while unseen (Layers of Fear, Antichamber), change between loops or visits (P.T.), change as a discrete anomaly against a stable baseline (The Exit 8 / Platform 8), and change synced to music (Control's Ashtray Maze, GDC 2020 talk). Two technical contrasts help. Superliminal's graphics programmer writes that the illusion is ruined "if lighting shifts at all", which supports the user's rule. Splatoon is the opposite: the patent puts the ink texture over the stage texture, Nintendo raised the ink's own specular intensity, and the team tried removing shading so ink edges read clearly. In Splatoon the overlay owns its material; in the user's design the moving layer must own none. For the 1990 era lock, plausible diegetic frames are Hypercolor thermochromic dye (1991), blacklight/DayGlo fluorescent inks (1930s onward), lenticular (Vari-Vue, trademark 1953), Magic Eye (Japan 1991, first US book 1993: a hidden figure encoded in a repeating pattern), Anaglypta/Lincrusta paintable relief papers (1887/1877: the relief is separate from the colour) and rotating-prism signs (US3199239, 1965). Project-specific finding: Tools/lookdev/gen_surfaces.py currently bakes the chevron ink into the normal (0.9*blur(ink)), smoothness (+0.07*ink) and cavity (-0.10*ink). If the graphic moves, the old chevron will show as a ghost in the specular. That should either be removed or kept on purpose as Gilman's "sub-pattern". Not verified: any wallpaper pattern shift in A24's Backrooms (2026) (none found; Phantasmag interview not located, Gold Derby paywalled); Marathon's Gantry "flickering graffiti textures" (no primary source); all video timestamps.

findings.topic: Literature - The Yellow Wallpaper (Charlotte Perkins Gilman, 1892, New England Magazine)
findings.claim: Gilman's wallpaper is a literal two-layer sandwich: a front pattern and a sub-pattern seen only in certain light, which moves by moonlight and stays still by day.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Project Gutenberg #1952 text). Passages: the paper has a 'sub-pattern in a different shade' that you 'can only see in certain lights'; by moonlight the narrator would not know it was the same paper; at night the outside pattern 'becomes bars' and the woman behind is plain to see; 'The front pattern does move... The woman behind shakes it!'; and a streak runs round the room low on the wall. What changes: the visible pattern's motion and readability. Trigger: the kind of light (moonlight vs. daylight) and time of day. Lighting is not neutral here: the light reveals the hidden layer. FRONTROOMS LESSON (inference): the motion layer can be keyed to light state (troffer flicker/off) while shading stays on the paper. A faint static emboss of the 'original' chevron left in the paper normal would literally be a sub-pattern visible only in certain (grazing/specular) light.

findings.topic: Film/TV - The Yellow Wallpaper (BBC, 1989)
findings.claim: A BBC TV adaptation starring Julia Watson aired in 1989, inside FrontRooms' diegetic era.
findings.detail: PARTLY VERIFIED: Julia Watson's Wikipedia filmography lists 'The Yellow Wallpaper' (1989) under Television. The director credit (John Clive) and the summary ('imagine that there is a woman behind the paper') come from search excerpts (Hypatia Trust, Shmoop); the Wellesley catalogue record returned 403. Not watched; no timestamp. LESSON: a period-true screen version of the 'figure behind the pattern' existed in 1989, so it is a legitimate in-era reference for the deck.

findings.topic: Web series - Backrooms (Kane Pixels / Kane Parsons, 2022-)
findings.claim: The Backrooms source canon names The Yellow Wallpaper directly and already treats deformed wallpaper as an anomaly.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Wikipedia episode list). First video 'The Backrooms (Found Footage)' was posted Jan 7 2022, made in Blender and After Effects, and is set mainly in the early 1990s (Async discovers the Backrooms in the late 1980s). Episode 13 '9780415263573' (May 20 2022) is titled with the ISBN of The Yellow Wallpaper. Episode 24 'Static Dead End' (Feb 12 2025) has researchers recording 'stretched wallpaper, irregular floor depth, and furniture phased into the walls and flooring'. Timestamps not verified. LESSON: a moving or stretching print is on-canon for the Backrooms and in-era for 1990. Episode 24 is the closest original footage to cite first.

findings.topic: Film - Backrooms (A24, 2026; dir. Kane Parsons; PD Danny Vermette; VFX sup. Edward J. Douglas)
findings.claim: The production tested many chevron/carpet/lighting combinations to stop the pattern 'striating' on camera. No source found describes the wallpaper pattern animating or shifting.
findings.detail: VERIFIED: Galerie says Vermette ran about 50 camera tests of yellow chevron variants so the pattern would not distort or striate at scale. It also says the 2019 source photo was a beige chevron that looked yellow because of a white-balance error, and that the team burnt out printer heads on custom wallpaper from a Vancouver supplier. W Magazine gives 30,000 sq ft of wallpaper and 27,000 sq ft of carpet and describes a palette shift from greys/blues through beige into yellow. Sources disagree on test counts (30 vs ~50) and wallpaper area (30k/32k/37k sq ft). Douglas's VIEW Conference talk covers set extension, a full CG pipeline expanding Parsons' Blender process, and 'No-Clipping effects'. motionpictures.org says the portals were practical, with separate portals for actor and camera plus roto. NOT VERIFIED: any in-film wallpaper pattern shift. The Phantasmag interview was not located, Gold Derby is paywalled (402), Dezeen returned 403, and the Blu-ray VFX breakdowns (5m, 2m, 16m) were not viewed. LESSON: a static high-contrast chevron already aliases on camera; a moving one will shimmer more. Plan anti-aliasing and filtering for the motion layer from day one.

findings.topic: Film - The Shining (1980, Stanley Kubrick): hexagon carpet 'reversal'
findings.claim: In the hallway toy scene the carpet pattern appears reversed for one shot because Danny and the camera were moved, not the carpet.
findings.detail: VERIFIED as a documented observation: moviemistakes lists it as a continuity error. Idyllopus Press analyses shots 257-259 (shot 257 shows a reversed hexagon field; 258 returns to normal) and argues 'Kubrick has moved Danny' one diagonal step, with a visible white wall edge as the orientation clue. Intentionality is the author's interpretation. Lighting is unchanged across the shots. LESSON (inference): the cheapest 'motion graphic' is no new art at all. Offsetting or mirroring the graphic layer's world-planar UV by half a repeat flips the read of the pattern while the paper and lighting stay the same.

findings.topic: Film - Repulsion (1965, Roman Polanski)
findings.claim: Walls of the flat crack open and hands reach out of the corridor walls as Carol's mind breaks down.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Wikipedia): Polanski uses 'explicitly expressionistic effects (cracks suddenly ripping through walls, rough hands reaching out...)'; art director Seamus Flannery, cinematographer Gilbert Taylor. NOT VERIFIED: how the effects were built. Here the wall surface itself fails rather than its print changing. LESSON: the escalation after 'the pattern moves' is 'the paper and wall break', which belongs to the texture layer and geometry, not the graphic layer.

findings.topic: Film - Barton Fink (1991, Coen brothers; PD Dennis Gassner)
findings.claim: The Hotel Earle's wallpaper (printed with rotting banana leaves) progressively comes unglued in the heat.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (AFI Catalog): Gassner's 'distressed' Art Deco look, which Joel Coen called 'organic' and 'decayed', used wallpaper depicting 'rotting brown banana leaves'. Barton notices 'a piece of wallpaper coming unglued', and later 'more strips of wallpaper come unglued'. The film is from 1991, inside the era lock. Paste oozing from the wall is widely described but not verified here. LESSON: decay belongs to the paper (texture) layer and progresses over time, separately from the print. FrontRooms' macro wear already lives on this side of the sandwich.

findings.topic: Film - A Nightmare on Elm Street (1984, Wes Craven)
findings.claim: Freddy stretches through the wall above Nancy's bed. The wall was a spandex membrane with effects artist Jim Doyle pushing through from behind.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Wikipedia): Doyle's 'face and hands... stretch through the wall and reach out for Nancy when she dreams; the wall was built by Doyle out of spandex.' This is the practical-effects version of Gilman's 'the woman behind shakes it': the hidden layer deforms the skin. LESSON: the one deliberate exception to the user's rule. For rare scripted beats, let the motion layer push into the paper layer's normal or vertices (a bulge). Normally the paper ignores it.

findings.topic: Film VFX - Silent Hill (2006), BUF Compagnie (VFX sup. Stephane Ceretti)
findings.claim: The fog-world walls were treated as a skin over the Darkness world. Both set versions were rebuilt in 3D and the skin was peeled with cloth dynamics in a spreading, reversible transition.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Prix Ars Electronica 2007, Honorary Mention): 'The walls of Silent Hill turn from fog world to darkness world. This transformation looks like a disease spreading through the city.' Both set versions were reconstructed in 3D, with cloth dynamics making walls buckle and fall and propagation tuned per shot. SIGGRAPH 2007 Computer Animation Festival lists BUF's making-of. AWN's article (403) adds via search excerpt: tracked on top of each other, fractal-driven progression, run in reverse for Darkness-to-fog. LESSON: when the change should be material (paper peeling to reveal something else), use two full material states plus a spreading mask. That is a separate event from the albedo-only sandwich.

findings.topic: Game - Layers of Fear (Bloober Team, 2016)
findings.claim: The house reshapes itself when the player looks away, and paintings transform.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Steam store): 'the unstable environment reacts to your fragile state of mind, reshaping itself when you look away'; world inspired by 19th-century paintings and decor. Reviews describe paintings fading and transforming in view. Trigger: leaving the camera view. Lighting stays consistent because swaps happen unseen. No technical talk found. LESSON: off-screen swaps. FrontRooms' wallpaper is world-projected and shared by every wall, so a swap needs a per-wall or per-region mask; otherwise changing an unseen wall also changes the visible ones.

findings.topic: Game - P.T. (Kojima Productions, 2014, Fox Engine)
findings.claim: A looping hallway is redecorated on each loop with changed lighting, objects and framed pictures.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Wikipedia): released Aug 12 2014; after each loop 'lighting shifts to red, objects appear or vanish'. Secondary analysis says a framed picture changes on one loop, and in another the hallway is lined with frames of 'vibrating human eyes'. Trigger: re-entering the loop, off-screen. LESSON: change between visits. FrontRooms streams a 3x3 chunk ring, so a chunk re-entering the ring can return in a new graphic state with no on-screen transition.

findings.topic: Game - The Exit 8 (Kotake Create, 2023) / Platform 8 (2024)
findings.claim: Anomaly-spotting loops: signs, posters and light patterns change against an otherwise identical corridor.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Wikipedia): UE5; released Nov 29 2023. Anomalies include 'different messages on signs, repeating poster designs', power outages and an irregular fluorescent pattern. Turn back on an anomaly and succeed 8 times in a row. Platform 8 (May 31 2024) moves the idea to an endless train. Automaton interviews cover design, including anomalies cut for being too hard. LESSON: a pattern change only works as gameplay against a perfectly stable baseline. Keep the base wallpaper deterministic so a changed graphic reads as an anomaly, not as noise.

findings.topic: Game - Control (Remedy, 2019): Ashtray Maze
findings.claim: A shifting, heavily animated maze section synced to music. Remedy presented it at the GDC 2020 Level Design Summit.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Game Developer / GDC listing): talk 'Designing the Ashtray Maze in Control' by Anne-Marie Gronroos covers modularity, 'fast prototyping of heavily animated environments' and the constraints of a musical sequence. 80.lv (Jan 6 2020) relays game director Mikael Kasurinen saying the maze began as a lock to block progress. Vault video not viewed. LESSON: the environment's change can be driven by an audio timeline. FrontRooms' FMOD (sound chat) could drive the motion layer's phase.

findings.topic: Game - Antichamber (Alexander Bruce, 2013, UE3)
findings.claim: Passages and structures change depending on which way the player faces (view-dependent space).
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Wikipedia): released Jan 31 2013; Bruce says breaking and remaking expectations 'is essentially the core mechanic'. GDC 2014 IGS talk 'Antichamber: An Overnight Success, Seven Years in the Making' is a postmortem without render-tech detail. LESSON: view-direction-gated change is an established first-person language. It pairs with frustum and visibility checks for wallpaper swaps.

findings.topic: Game - Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice (Ninja Theory, 2017)
findings.claim: Rune puzzles: the player finds arrangements of objects or light that match gate runes when seen from a particular angle (pareidolia).
findings.detail: PARTLY VERIFIED: Wikipedia confirms environment pattern-matching puzzles tied to Senua's perception. The 'particular angle' description comes from Giant Bomb's wiki via search excerpt (page 403). No primary dev source found. LESSON: a hidden figure that appears only from one viewpoint is a game-readable form of Gilman's sub-pattern.

findings.topic: Game tech - Superliminal (Pillow Castle, 2019): trompe-l'oeil wall paintings
findings.claim: The graphics programmer states that a painted-on illusion is ruined if lighting shifts at all when it changes.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (PlayStation Blog, Jun 30 2020, Phil Fortier). They render an object from a viewport and project that image back from the same viewpoint, and must 'take great care when capturing images' because 'if the object goes from 2D to real 3D, the illusion will be ruined if lighting shifts at all.' LESSON: direct support for the user's rule. If swapping the graphic changes shading, players see the trick. Keep all specular, normal and cavity response on the static paper layer.

findings.topic: Game - Viewfinder (Sad Owl Studios, 2023)
findings.claim: 2D images (photos, drawings) are mapped onto the 3D world, creating new geometry.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Wikipedia): PS5/PC release Jul 18 2023; the core mechanic maps images from photographs and other 2D works into 3D space. No render breakdown found. LESSON: low relevance to the sandwich. It shows an image layer acting as world-changing data, a possible later puzzle layer.

findings.topic: Game tech - Splatoon / Splatoon 2 (Nintendo)
findings.claim: Splatoon renders a paint texture over the stage texture (100% paint colour where inked) and then lights it. Nintendo gave the ink its own higher specular, the inverse of the user's sandwich.
findings.detail: VERIFIED: Nintendo patent US12482186B2 (filed Jul 21 2023, published Nov 25 2025). The stage mesh uses a stage texture and a paint texture; 'the paint texture is prioritized over the stage texture', rendered with 0% stage colour and 100% paint colour, then lighting is applied. Nintendo's recruit page on Splatoon 2: they adopted PBR, raised ink specular intensity for sparkle, tried removing shading to make ink borders easier to tell apart, and put playability first. No CEDEC ink-rendering talk was found (Splatoon won 3 CEDEC Awards in 2016). LESSON: in Splatoon the overlay owns its material (glossy ink on top). In FrontRooms the moving layer sits under the paper and must own no material at all. Splatoon's readability tweak also suggests a moving print may need lower shading contrast to stay legible.

findings.topic: Game tech - Portal 2 gel (Valve, 2011)
findings.claim: Gel is stored in per-surface 'paintmaps' whose resolution follows the surface's lightmap scale, a separate layer at its own resolution.
findings.detail: VERIFIED via search excerpt only (the Valve Developer Community page returned 403 to the fetcher). Gel uses generated paintmaps scaled by lightmap scale; maps need compiled lighting; worldspawn needs 'Paint in Map' set. LESSON: the changing layer does not need the static material's resolution. The chevron graphic is low-frequency and could be a small texture or a procedural; paper fibre stays at 2048x3072.

findings.topic: Game - Marathon (Bungie, 2026): Gantry
findings.claim: UNVERIFIED: no primary source found for 'flickering graffiti-like textures' on Gantry.
findings.detail: Gantry exists as a MIDA faction figure in coverage, and Marathon launched Mar 5 2026 (Wikipedia). The 'constantly shifting visuals, graffiti-like textures flickering across his mannequin-like figure' description appeared only in a search engine's summary with no attributable page. The Wikipedia article does not mention it. Verified related context: art director Joseph Cross defines 'graphic realism' as simplified design language, strong graphic design and colour statements, and limited materials (80.lv, May 30 2023). Do not cite the Gantry claim until a trailer timestamp or official page is found.

findings.topic: Games - Anemoiapolis / Escape the Backrooms (and Observation, Kentucky Route Zero, Amnesia)
findings.claim: No wallpaper-pattern-change mechanic was found in these titles.
findings.detail: Anemoiapolis is by solo developer Andrew Quist, inspired by 2020 liminal-space and Backrooms posts (Steam app 1522960). Escape the Backrooms (Fancy Games; 1.0 on Oct 23) has a Level 0 with peeling yellowed wallpaper and humming fluorescents (secondary sources). No pattern-animation feature found. Observation, Kentucky Route Zero and Amnesia were not researched in depth; no evidence collected. Treat them as genre and mood references, not sandwich precedents.

findings.topic: Theme-park illusion - Haunted Mansion (Disneyland, opened Aug 12 1969)
findings.claim: The strongest trigger precedent: portraits flicker into macabre versions when lightning flashes, and the Stretching Room's portraits elongate to reveal their subjects' grim fates.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Wikipedia): Stretching Room is an elevator; as the room stretches 'the portrait frames appear to elongate, revealing the subjects' grim but humorous fates' (portraits by Marc Davis). In the corridor, 'the subjects of the portraits... flicker briefly into macabre versions of themselves when lightning flashes from the windows'. WDWNT says the Magic Kingdom lightning portrait scene was added in 2007 and made more vibrant in 2019. NOT VERIFIED: the technique; sources conflict among lenticular, rear-projection slide-fades and electroluminescent. Ride footage not timestamped. LESSON: hide or justify the swap inside a lighting event. FrontRooms' independently flickering troffers act as the lightning: change the graphic only within a fixture's footprint during its off or flicker frames.

findings.topic: Real-world - E Ink Prism (E Ink Holdings, CES Jan 2015)
findings.claim: A bistable E Ink film for walls and architectural materials that changes colour and pattern, triggered by a switch or by sensors for noise, temperature or motion.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (TechXplore, Jan 7 2015): 'bistable ink technology in a film that can transform architectural materials into dynamic designs'; 'Programmable patterns and shapes'; walls 'can respond to noise, temperature, or motion in the room'; low power. A search excerpt (Reviewed.com) describes the CES wall of tiles rippling pink/red octagons. LESSON: a real 'motion wallpaper' whose pigment layer sits under a clear front film, so sheen belongs to the top film. Bistable means change then hold, which suggests step changes over continuous loops. Not diegetic for 1990 (modern technology); use as a technical analogy only.

findings.topic: Real-world - BMW iX Flow featuring E Ink (CES, Jan 5 2022)
findings.claim: A body wrap of laser-cut ePaper segments shaped by generative design changes the car's colour. It uses no energy to hold a state.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (BMW Group press release): 'many precisely fitted ePaper segments'; 'Laser cutting technologies'; 'Generative design processes... ensure the segments reflect the characteristic contours'; microcapsules with charged white and black pigments; current only flows during the change. CORRECTION to the task premise: BMW describes a wrap of ePaper segments, not E Ink under paint or clear coat; a clear coat is not verified. LESSON: segment the changing layer along the surface's own grid. In FrontRooms that grid is the 0.75 m roll strips, so switch the graphic strip by strip and respect seams.

findings.topic: Real-world - Philips + Kvadrat Soft Cells 'Luminous Textile' (Jul 4 2011)
findings.claim: Addressable RGB LEDs behind tensioned acoustic fabric show dynamic content while the fabric's texture stays visible: a literal fabric-over-image sandwich.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Signify/Philips press release, Jul 4 2011): Philips' addressable LEDs integrated into Kvadrat Soft Cells panels; 'display of dynamic visual content'; aluminium frame keeps the fabric surface 'perfectly stretched'. A 37 m2 installation was shown in Dresden (LEDinside). LESSON: this image is emissive (it glows through the fabric) and is unaffected by room light. The user's design is reflective albedo, lit by room light. Decide which one FrontRooms wants: it changes how the layer behaves when a troffer flickers off.

findings.topic: Real-world - Meystyle LED wallpaper (Maria & Ekaterina Yaschuk; prototype 2004, company 2007)
findings.claim: Meystyle integrates LEDs into the wallpaper material itself, digitally printed on non-woven and hung like normal wallcovering.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Wikipedia): MA Textile Futures prototype at Central Saint Martins in 2004; 'Wire Geometrics' shown in 2007; Meystyle claims to be first to 'fully integrate light-emitting diodes into the material of the wallpaper so that it can be hung like a traditional wall covering'; Maison&Objet Projects Award 2014. LESSON: precedent for an active layer inside paper. Post-1990, so a technical analogy only.

findings.topic: Real-world - Shi Yuan, heat-sensitive (thermochromic) wallpaper (by Jan 2008)
findings.claim: A printed wallpaper whose green leaves bloom into red flowers as a nearby heat source (e.g. a radiator) warms it.
findings.detail: VERIFIED via secondary sources: Adactio links (Jan 11 2008) points to shiyuan.co.uk and singles out 'the heat-sensitive wallpaper with blooming flowers'; Brit+Co (Jan 6 2012): 'As the temperature changes in the room, these green leaves blossom into red flowers.' TrendHunter's page returned 403; the designer's portfolio was not opened. LESSON: thermochromic ink makes 'only the print changes, the paper stays' physically real. Trigger: heat.

findings.topic: Real-world - Sibren Drenthen, 'Wallpaper 3.0' (Design Academy Eindhoven, 2019)
findings.claim: Flowers embroidered with thermochromic yarn on wallpaper change colour when heated by motion-activated foil, a three-layer sandwich.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Design Academy Eindhoven graduation page): 'flowers embroidered onto the wallpaper with heat-sensitive thermo-chromic yarn' heated by motion-activated foil; 'a shade-shifting, transformative surface that reacts directly to the surroundings'. LESSON: a working stack of heater (trigger), paper (static texture) and thermochromic thread (changing graphic), triggered by a passer-by's motion. That is a ready analogy for proximity-triggered changes.

findings.topic: Projection art - Pablo Valbuena, 'Augmented Sculpture v1.2' (Medialab-Prado / Ars Electronica, 2007)
findings.claim: An early projection-mapping work defined explicitly as two overlapped layers: a physical layer and a virtual projected layer that controls transformation.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Ars Electronica festival archive): the physical layer 'controls the real space and shapes the volumetric base'; the virtual layer 'allows controlling the transformation and sequentiality of space-time'. LESSON: it names the user's sandwich. The projected layer must be registered exactly to the physical one. In FrontRooms the graphic layer must use the same world-planar frame (PlanarFrame, 192 m origin multiples) and 0.75 x 1.125 m tile so streaming chunks never disagree.

findings.topic: Real-world / 1990-plausible - Lenticular printing (Vari-Vue, trademark Dec 1953)
findings.claim: A ridged clear lens sheet over an interlaced print makes the image flip or animate with viewing angle. The lens on top owns the gloss and the print beneath changes.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Wikipedia): lenses 'accurately aligned with the interlaces of the image'; 'flip effect' and animation from sequential images; Vari-Vue trademark registered Dec 1953 and liquidated in 1988. Vari-Vue coined 'lenticular'. LESSON: a period-plausible diegetic explanation for a print that changes with viewpoint. It is also the cleanest physical model of the sandwich: top-layer specular, bottom-layer albedo.

findings.topic: 1990 era - Hypercolor (Generra Sportswear, debut Jan 1991)
findings.claim: Mass-market thermochromic clothing (leuco dye from Matsui Shikiso) changed colour with body heat. It sold $50M between Feb and May 1991.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Wikipedia): Generra of Seattle; leuco dye (crystal violet lactone) system switching at about 24-27 C; the effect could be permanently damaged by hot washing or ironing; Generra went bankrupt in 1992. LESSON: the most era-exact diegetic frame (1991) for 'the print changes, the paper doesn't'. Triggers: hands, breath, lamps. Permanent damage suggests 'burned-in' states that never revert.

findings.topic: 1990 era - Magic Eye autostereograms (N.E. Thing Enterprises; Japan 1991, first US book 1993)
findings.claim: A hidden 3D figure is encoded inside a repeating colour pattern by shifting the repeat horizontally according to a depth map.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (AIGA Eye on Design): Tom Baccei and Cheri Smith, named with Tenyo in Japan in 1991; first US book by Andrews McMeel in 1993 (30,000-copy run sold out within 24 hours); the method is a depth map plus a repeating 'starter strip' shifted per depth. Inside the <=1993 era lock. LESSON: formally the same as Gilman's woman behind the pattern. A motion layer could hide a figure by modulating the repeat period, readable only by attentive players.

findings.topic: 1990 era - DayGlo / blacklight fluorescent inks (Switzer brothers, 1930s-)
findings.claim: Black-light fluorescent paints (1930s) and daylight fluorescent pigments (1940s) were long established by 1990 for posters and displays.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Wikipedia, DayGlo): the Switzers used black light to find fluorescent compounds and 'invented the first black light fluorescent paints' by mixing them with shellac; then fluorescent paints for movie posters and advertising displays; daylight-fluorescent pigments from the 1940s. LESSON: a period-true 'second print' that is invisible under normal light and appears under UV. Inference: a blacklight tube or ballast fault is a plausible in-world trigger for revealing a hidden graphic layer.

findings.topic: Period wallpaper material - Anaglypta (1887) / Lincrusta (1877)
findings.claim: Paintable relief wallcoverings show that a wallpaper's relief (texture) and its colour are physically separate layers.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Wikipedia): Lincrusta was launched in 1877 by Frederick Walton (linseed-oil paste); Anaglypta was invented by Thomas J. Palmer, made from wood pulp and cotton, produced from 1887, 'a range of paintable textured wallcoverings'. Modern patents describe 'in-register' embossing, where emboss is aligned to a pre-printed design on PVC wallcoverings. LESSON (inference): FrontRooms' generator currently makes an in-register emboss (chevron baked into height and normal). If the ink moves, the emboss becomes off-register: an uncanny 'ghost' of where the pattern used to be. Remove it, or keep it deliberately as Gilman's sub-pattern.

findings.topic: 1990 era - Rotating triangular-prism signs (Trivision type)
findings.claim: Mechanical multi-message signs using rotating three-sided vanes were patented in 1965.
findings.detail: VERIFIED (Google Patents US3199239A, 'Rotatable Indicia-Bearing Vanes for Signboards', Theodore M. Reed, filed Jun 11 1963, granted Aug 10 1965). How common they were by 1990 is not verified. LESSON: a period-plausible mechanical 'changing print'. Inference: a transition where each 0.75 m roll strip flips in sequence reads as 1990 machinery, not a screen.

findings.topic: SYNTHESIS (inference) - Physical sandwiches put the sheen on top; FrontRooms' current bake does not
findings.claim: Every real sandwich found (E Ink film, lenticular lens, Luminous Textile, Meystyle, Drenthen) puts reflection and gloss on the static top layer, so the user's rule is physically sound. FrontRooms' wallpaper bake currently ties the chevron ink into the normal, smoothness and cavity.
findings.detail: Project fact (read-only check): Tools/lookdev/gen_surfaces.py wallpaper() lines 68-71 build height with 0.9*blur(ink), smoothness with +0.07*blur(ink), and cavity with -0.10*ink. FrontRoomsSurface.shader samples _BaseMap, _BumpMap and _MaskMap with one shared world-planar UV (line 183) before UniversalFragmentPBR. Consequence (inference): animating only the albedo leaves the old chevron fixed in the normal and specular. That is a bug unless chosen as the Gilman 'sub-pattern'. wallpaper_cold() is already described as 'the same paper under a different print run', a static two-state version of the idea. Rendering files belong to the visual chat.

findings.topic: SYNTHESIS (inference) - Trigger taxonomy drawn from the precedents
findings.claim: The precedents give five tested triggers for a changing surface: a light event, out of view, between visits, an environmental sensor, and music.
findings.detail: Light event: Haunted Mansion lightning portraits, Gilman's moonlight; maps to troffer flicker. Out of view: Layers of Fear, Antichamber. Between visits: P.T. loops; maps to chunk re-entry into the 3x3 ring. Sensor (noise, temperature, motion, heat): E Ink Prism, Hypercolor, Shi Yuan, Drenthen. Music: Control's Ashtray Maze; maps to FMOD. Cadence: bistable E Ink and Exit 8's discrete anomalies suggest step changes with long holds; continuous looping reads as a screen, which breaks the 1990 lock. Reserve continuous 'crawl' for scripted Gilman beats.

recommendations: Lead the research frame with original sources, per the user's rule: (1) Gilman's text, quoting the 'sub-pattern... only in certain lights' and 'woman behind shakes it' passages; (2) Kane Pixels episode 24 'Static Dead End' (stretched wallpaper) and episode 13 (the Yellow Wallpaper ISBN); (3) Haunted Mansion lightning changing-portraits ride footage; (4) the E Ink Prism CES 2015 and BMW iX Flow CES 2022 videos; (5) BUF's Silent Hill making-of; (6) Layers of Fear and Exit 8 gameplay. Timestamps were NOT verified, so capture the clips and log URLs and timecodes in SOURCES.md before using them.

Adopt the Haunted Mansion trigger as the primary mechanic: change the wallpaper graphic only inside a troffer's footprint during its off or flicker frames. Shading never changes, so the swap reads as 'the light lied' rather than a texture pop. This needs coordination with the visual chat, which owns the shader and light code.

Ask the visual chat to split Tools/lookdev/gen_surfaces.py wallpaper() into paper-only maps (fibre, mottling, seams, foxing in normal/mask) plus a separate ink mask. Then decide on purpose whether a faint static emboss of the 'original' chevron stays in the paper normal as Gilman's sub-pattern, visible only at grazing or specular angles.

Register the motion layer to the existing world-planar frame (PlanarFrame, 0.75 x 1.125 m tile, 192 m origin multiples). Drive its state from world position plus global time or event IDs so that chunks streaming in or out never disagree. Change it per 0.75 m roll strip, following BMW's segments and the prism signs.

Prefer discrete, bistable state changes with long holds over continuous animation for Level 0, as the E Ink and Exit 8 precedents suggest. Reserve slow continuous 'crawl' and the Nightmare/Gilman 'something pushes from behind' normal bulge for rare scripted beats; that bulge is the only place the motion layer may touch the paper's lighting.

For in-fiction 1990 framing, use thermochromic ink (Hypercolor 1991), UV/blacklight fluorescent ink (DayGlo) or lenticular print. Do not use E Ink or LED wallpaper diegetically, since they postdate 1993; keep them as engineering analogies.

Budget for anti-aliasing early. The Backrooms film needed dozens of camera tests to stop a static chevron striating; a moving chevron at 0.75 m under 4x MSAA will shimmer at distance. Use mip-mapped flipbooks or analytically filtered procedural edges, and keep visible motion inside the roughly 20 m fog range.

Decide whether the motion layer is reflective albedo (lit by the troffers, goes dark when they die) or emissive (glows through the paper like Luminous Textile, visible in blackouts). It is the main design fork the precedents expose.
